12 Angry Actors Left Me Guilty of One Thing: Not Having an Answer

  • August 21, 2026
  • ganish kapur
SHARE this
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:48
Instaread

I walked into Meat Market Stables in North Melbourne expecting a night of theatre. I walked out with a headache I didn’t want to lose, the good kind, the kind that keeps you awake replaying a stranger’s monologue at 2am, arguing with yourself in the dark.

That’s 12 Angry Actors for you.

A Rehearsal Room That Becomes a Courtroom

The premise sounds almost playful on paper: a play within a play. Twelve actors, gathered to rehearse a production, slowly discover that one of their own, a fellow cast member, served twenty years for manslaughter. He killed his wife. By accident, we’re told. But twenty years is twenty years, and once the secret is out, the rehearsal room stops being about blocking and line readings and becomes something closer to a trial.

Except there’s no judge. Just eleven other actors, and an audience, trying to work out the verdict for themselves.

What got me from the opening scenes was how funny it is before it isn’t. There’s real warmth and comic timing in the ensemble banter early on, which makes the gut-punch later hit even harder, because you’ve already fallen a little in love with these people before you’re forced to watch them turn on each other.

Everyone’s Righteous, and Everyone’s Right

The genius of the writing, courtesy of Brian Vriends and Celine Khoury, is that no character is simply “for” or “against” forgiveness. Every position on stage is built from a wound.

There’s the actor playing a criminal defence lawyer, performed by Celine Khoury herself, who – plot twist – actually is an award-winning criminal defence lawyer in real life. On stage, her character argues fiercely that people deserve second chances, that a debt paid is a debt paid. But she’s not smug about it. You can see her flinching at her own logic, wrestling with the unbearable thought: what if I’m wrong? What if I hand someone their freedom and they go on to hurt someone else? Is that on me?

I couldn’t stop wondering, sitting in the dark: does Khoury carry that same tension into courtrooms in her actual day job? Does a defence lawyer ever go home and lie awake with that same doubt? The play doesn’t answer that for us, but it made me want to ask her directly.

Then there’s another actor, a character shaped by a childhood watching his father cycle in and out of prison for beating his mother, only to come home and do it again. For him, “second chances” isn’t a philosophical debate. It’s a memory with bruises on it. His hostility toward the man with the criminal past isn’t cruelty, it’s self-preservation, forged years before he ever set foot in that rehearsal room.

By the interval, I realised the play wasn’t really about one man’s guilt. It was a room full of mirrors, each character reflecting back a different, entirely reasonable, entirely incompatible idea of what justice should look like.

The Ensemble Carrying It

None of this lands without a cast capable of holding that much nuance at once, and this one does. The ensemble includes Ursula Searle, Ali Samaei, Alexander Given, Celine Khoury, Claire Warrillow, Monty Burgess, Faouzi Daghistani, Joanna Karanikolopoulos, Esther B Ebony, Kathy Richer and Jacob Saunders, who each get a moment to make their character’s logic feel unshakeable, right up until the next person dismantles it.

The Monologue That Undid the Room

Then comes the moment the whole play has been building toward, the accused actor finally speaks for himself.

He doesn’t ask for pity. He tells his story plainly: the wife he lost, the life that ended the day hers did, and the fact that the people now judging him have never once had to survive what he’s had to survive. But it’s the line about prison that stayed with me longest. He says prison, in a strange way, was simple, you’re told exactly what’s expected of you, you follow the rules, and you get through the day. It’s the world outside the walls that’s unforgiving. Nobody hands you a rulebook for how to be forgiven. You’re just supposed to know, and you’re punished again and again for getting it wrong.

Twenty years of paying a debt, and society still isn’t sure it’s been paid.

The room went completely silent. I don’t think anyone was checking their phone during that scene.

Then They Handed Us the Verdict

At the very end, the audience votes. Should he be given a genuine second chance, or not?

I voted. I’m still not sure I believe my own vote.

That’s the real achievement of 12 Angry Actors, it refuses to let you leave with a clean conscience either way. Say yes, and some part of you wonders if you’re being naive. Say no, and you have to sit with what that means about who gets to be human again, and who doesn’t. There’s no applause-line answer. Just the uncomfortable, necessary questions: Where does punishment actually end? Who decides when someone has earned their way back? Do our morals have edges, or do we just pretend they do until we’re the ones being asked to forgive?

Why This Play Is Going to Stay With Me

12 Angry Actors doesn’t hand you a moral. It doesn’t tell you punishment is pointless or that forgiveness is always earned. It just keeps asking, quietly and then not so quietly: when does it end? Who gets to decide? And do our morals actually have limits, or do we just like to think they do?

I still don’t have clean answers. I’m not sure the writers do either, and I think that’s exactly why this production, seven years in the making by Vriends and Khoury, works as well as it does.

This isn’t Asamina Theatre Company’s first swing at a big, morally knotty story, their earlier production Son of Byblos showed the same appetite for tackling difficult material with heart. But 12 Angry Actors feels like a step up.

“Asamina Theatre Company, formerly The Thespian Theatre Company, is making a breakthrough with 12 Angry Actors. I have seen a few of their past works. For the quality they delivered with this latest production, it’s time for Asamina to be in a bigger space with a proper stage!” ~ Roslyn Foo

If you’re in Melbourne before the run ends, go. Bring someone you can argue with afterwards over a drink, because you will need to.

12 Angry Actors is playing at Meat Market Stables, North Melbourne, until 30 August 2026.

Tickets and Details: eventbrite.com.au

Follow Along: Asamina Theatre Company
